note: Read from tree-sitter-swift's scanner.c. The memory is one `uint32_t` -
`ongoing_raw_str_hash_count` - and the census read that as a single mark whose
count is how many `#` opened the raw string being read. Everything else this
scanner does is a decision over the bytes at the offset and the permission set,
which is why swift is the grammar where `Provision` already got furthest.
It got furthest and it is now gone: the nineteen rows it held are the
`roll:` rules below. A `Provision` was a spelling plus the trailing bytes
its scanner refuses, seated as an ordinary slate pattern, and the seat was
the approximation. `eat_operators` reads `valid_symbols` BEFORE it collects
candidates, so a fixed operator competes only where its own terminal is
wanted; a slate pattern competes everywhere and is filtered after the fact.
That difference is exactly what this book used to have to write down as a
limitation, and the paragraph that did is deleted below rather than
reworded, because the limitation is not there any more.
This book claims the four answers a pattern table structurally cannot reach:
_custom_operator   a decision about a WHOLE maximal operator run - is this
run one of the 31 RESERVED_OPS, exactly - which no fixed
pattern states, because the run's length is what is being
tested. This is the `..<` / `!=` pair the board reports:
`..<` is reserved and must stay the seated token, `!=` is
not and must be a custom operator.
_bang_custom       the twentieth row of OP_SYMBOLS, and the one the roll
named and declined: OP_SYMBOL_SUPPRESSOR conditions it
on FAKE_TRY_BANG *not* being wanted, and a Provision had
no access to a permission set. `not_wanted` is that test.
multiline_comment  nested, so the extent is a balanced run and not a
pattern. swift keeps the depth on the C stack through
recursion, which is the one place in the eight where
`serialize` under-reports the memory. A hand answers it
today and answers it right, so this rule is shadowed and
written down anyway: it is what the hand leaves behind.
raw_str_*          the family that reads the register: `#`-counting, and
the mark carries the count so the closer must match it.
The `roll:` rules are the nineteen, longest spelling first, because that is
`full_match`'s own preference: the C overwrites it with every longer candidate
that completes, so the answer is the longest wanted fixed operator whose
illegal-terminator group permits the byte after it. They stand ahead of the
two custom-operator rules for the same reason - `eat_operators` returns
`full_match` at scanner.c:658 and CUSTOM_OPERATOR only at 679.
What the move repaired, and it was a real wrong answer rather than a tidy-up:
`&&`, `||`, `??` and `==` are legal operator runs that are NOT in RESERVED_OPS,
so the C emits the fixed terminal where it is wanted and `custom_operator`
where it is not. The roll could answer only the first half, so this book had
to refuse all four lexically - a `no_probe roll_owns` guard on both custom
rules - and `a &&& b` was a stray. With the fixed rules present and gated on
`wanted`, a run the state refuses falls through to the custom rules the way it
falls through in the C, and the guard is deleted.

rules.name: raw_string_opens_and_shuts
rules.note: scanner.c:929-1004 read as ONE token, which is what it is. The opener is not a token: `eat_raw_str_part` counts the hashes, eats the quote, and then *falls through* into the body loop, so the answer that begins at `#"` ends either before an interpolation or on the last hash of the close. A book that emitted the opener alone reported every raw string as two answers where the tree holds one, and the delimiter width it never re-read let `##"a "# b"##` close on the inner `"#`. The backreference is the delimiter: `"\1` is a close only at the width that opened it, so the body crosses a shorter run without stopping. No mark, because a string that closes in one answer was never left open.

rules.name: raw_string_opens_into_interpolation
rules.note: scanner.c:993-998 reached from the `hash_count == 0` arm. Same one answer, stopped early: `\#(` at exactly the opening width ends the part *before* the backslash, which the C spells as a mark_end it declines to move. Mutually exclusive with the whole form by construction - neither body may cross the other's terminator - so which rule stands first says nothing. The mark is pushed here and only here, because this is the one arm that leaves the string open.

rules.name: raw_string_interpolates
rules.note: scanner.c:993-998 reached from the `RAW_STR_CONTINUING_INDICATOR` arm - the resumed part, after the interpolation's `)`. The width cannot be a backreference here because the opener is behind us, so the probe captures the run it found and the guard holds it to the mark: `\###(` inside a `#` string is not an interpolation, and the C declines it for the same reason - it counts at most `hash_count` hashes and then finds no `(`.

rules.name: raw_string_shuts
rules.note: scanner.c:999-1004. `"` then exactly the opening count of hashes, and the answer ends on the very last hash.

rules.name: nested_block_comment
rules.note: scanner.c:690-745. `nesting_depth` lives on the C stack, so `serialize` cannot see it and a fork mid-comment restarts at depth one. A balanced run states it without recursion, and an unterminated comment runs to end of input because the C answers it rather than refusing.

rules.name: bang_is_postfix_unless_try
rules.note: scanner.c:658-676 with OP_SYMBOL_SUPPRESSOR[BANG]. outside.zig declines this row by name because a Provision cannot ask whether `_fake_try_bang` is wanted. It is the only row of the twenty that needs the permission set to say NO, and this is that row.

rules.name: custom_operator_trims_trailing_angle
rules.note: scanner.c:679-682. A run whose last character is `<`, with anything but whitespace after it, answers one byte short - which is how `Array<Int>` keeps its bracket and `a +< b` does not. The lookbehind is on the maximal run, so a `<` in the middle of one is not mistaken for the end of it. The three refusals stand ahead of the run because a guard reads where the rule has read TO: behind it they would test the byte after the operator, and `...]` would pass a reserved check aimed at `]`.

rules.name: custom_operator
rules.note: scanner.c:679-685. `any_reserved_ops` is true only for a reserved op whose length is the run's length exactly - the C clears a match on the step after it - so the guard is `this run, whole, is not one of the 31`, which is the test no pattern in the roll can state.
